senses: The state of being a norm.
That which is normative.
To rub, especially to rub onto one surface placed upon another surface that is textured, in order to create a mottled or patterned area on the first surface.
ety: From French frottage (“rubbing”), from frotter (“to rub”) + -age (suffix forming nouns).

senses: A brandy from northern Spain, made from grapes.
An animal that has been recently weaned.
A device used to help wean a young animal by keeping it from suckling.
One who hunts foxes.
a dovecote, particularly a large one on an estate
That can be relocated.
Movable, but not functional/usable while being transported.
A strap-shaped structure.
Any metallic-looking sulphide, such as the above, which is the most common.
A person with golden hair, especially a girl with long hair.
A goldilocks aster (Aster linosyris).
ety: From goldy + locks. Goldilocks is a traditional children's story and its protagonist.

senses: The lightweight insulating material and aggregate resulting from expanding perlite glass by heat.
A track or path that follows the highest part of the landscape.
examples: A prehistoric ridgeway cuts across the parish, which contains two 19th-century turnpike tollhouses.

senses: Leave, formal permission for some action, (originally and particularly)
ety: From late Middle English congie, from Old French congié, congiet (modern French congé), from Latin commeātus (“passage, permission to leave”), from commeō (“to go and come”), from con- + meō (“to go, to pass”). Figurative senses generally borrowed from developments in French congé.

senses: A tomb; sepulchre.
A burial mound.
A camp; hill-fort.
ety: From Middle English bürȝen, from Old English byrġen, burġen (“burying-place, grave, sepulchre, tomb, burial”), from Proto-West Germanic *burginnju, from Proto-Germanic *burginjō (“burial”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰergʰ- (“to shelter, protect, save, preserve”). Related to Old English beorg (modern English barrow) and Old English byrġan (“to raise a mound, hide, bury, inter”). More at bury.

senses: Awesome, especially in the context of pets and other animals with paws.
Any bird in the order Psittaciformes: a parrot.
ety: From Ancient Greek ψιττακός (psittakós) + -ine. By surface analysis, psittac- + -ine.

senses: Unable to be won.
examples: This does mitigate the problem of the game playing itself, but it doesn't change the fact that at higher levels a lot of the games are either unwinnable or unloseable depending on the luck of "obey" or "disobey".

senses: Any of several techniques supposed to detect and modulate "life forces" and to provide healing using various electric black boxes.
ety: From radio- (“pertaining to rays or radiation”) + -onics.

senses: In labour, about to give birth, or having recently given birth.
About to create a new product, or float a new idea.
Of, related to, or caused by childbirth.
Facilitating labour.
ety: Borrowed from Latin parturiēns, present participle of parturiō (“to be in labour”).
examples: This communication is to develop this thought process as pertains to the position of the parturient woman during her delivery.

senses: The list of a newspaper's or another periodical's main staff, contributing writers, publisher, circulation, advertising rates etc.
The title (normally in a large and distinctive font, and at the top of the front page) of a newspaper or another periodical.
The publication itself, or the rights to publish it.
The logo of a broadcaster used in an ident.
examples: Maree said she felt worse after articles were written about the video, including by this masthead.

senses: Able to be hydrolyzed
Of a colour, produced by pigments.
An iron bucket used in mines for hoisting anything to the surface.
ety: From German Kübel (“pail”), from Middle High German kübel, kubel (“bucket, bushel, measure of grain”), from Old High German kubil (“tub, bucket”), from Proto-West Germanic *kubil, from Proto-Germanic *kub- (“to be vaulted, arch”), from Proto-Indo-European *gew-, *gū- (“to bend, curve, arch, vault”). Alternatively, possibly from Vulgar Latin *cupia, from Latin cūpa.

senses: A sales outlet which supplies goods or services over the World Wide Web.
To engage in dogfishing.
ety: From dog + fish. Compare Greek σκυλόψαρο (skylópsaro, “dogfish”), Latin canicula (“dogfish”, literally “little dog”), Italian pescecane (“dogfish”), French chien de mer (literally “dog of the sea”), German Meerhund (literally “seadog”) and Hundfisch (“dogfish”), and English seadog. For non-Indo-European cognates, see Maltese kelb il-baħar (literally “dog of the sea”) and Turkish köpek balığı (“shark”), likely calques from Indo-European languages.

senses: Having a violent or aggressive attitude towards men.
A law enforcement officer who specializes in disrupting organized crime.
Someone who hunts down a target in a manhunt.
A person who seeks men as sexual partners.
A dark-skinned variety of grape, used to produce red wines.
A wine produced from this variety of grape.
ety: Borrowed from French syrah. The derivation from the Persian city name of Shiraz (شیراز) is today believed to be a legend. The same goes for derivations from Syria, Syracuse or the Greek island of Syros. The name might be connected to the Celtic root Proto-Celtic *serrā, "billhook", referring to the method of harvesting.
examples: There will be organic beer from Anheuser-Busch and Six Gill syrah and Great White chardonnay from Shark Trust Wines, which gives 10 percent of its proceeds to help the endangered marine predators.

senses: An arc of the horizon intercepted between the meridian of the place and a vertical circle passing through the center of any object.
The quadrant of an azimuth circle.
ety: From Old French *azimut (modern French azimut), from Arabic اَلسُّمُوت pl (as-sumūt, “the directions”).

senses: A North-American hickory (Carya ovata) that has shaggy bark in mature trees; shagbark hickory
A West Indian leguminous tree, Pithecellobium micradenium.
examples: Trees such as the pin oak, the shagbark hickory, the linden, and the sugar maple are the arboreal equivalent of the high school student council.
They thought he was strong, tough, and resilient--just like the wood of the shagbark hickory tree, which is used to make athletic equipment today.
The face of the country is exceedingly beautiful, the soil fertile, and bearing oaks and shagbark hickory.

senses: A cat having orange- or ginger-colored fur.
ety: Borrowed from Middle French marmelade, from Portuguese marmelada (“quince jam”), from marmelo (“quince”), from Latin melimēlum (“sweet apple”), from Ancient Greek μελίμηλον (melímēlon), from μέλι (méli, “honey”) + μῆλον (mêlon, “apple”). A false folk etymology claims that this comes from the French phrase “Marie est malade” (“Mary is ill”), referring to Mary, Queen of Scots, falling ill and being given marmalade to feel better.

senses: An event held for fans.
examples: Fans of the genre frequently gather at comic book and sci-fi fanfests, which often screen Japanimation films.
Fanfests are increasingly popular, offering offseason weekends celebrating the team and its players and offering sponsors opportunities...
Since it's a fanfest, there are plenty of autographing and meet-the-musician events in beautiful, shady English Park...

senses: A unit of heat equal to 100,000 British thermal units, often used in the context of natural gas.
ety: 1920s, from Ancient Greek θερμός (thermós, “heat”). See also thermo-, -thermic, etc.

senses: A way or road dug through a hill, or sunk below the surface of the land.
Of wine, contaminated by a faulty or tainted cork.
Consisting of, or like, cork; dry; shrivelled.
examples: This wine smells a bit corky; get me another bottle.

senses: A badge of royalty, especially the early form of the pope's tiara.
ety: From Latin rēgnum (“kingdom”). Doublet of reign.

senses: Exhibiting symmetry around an axis; exhibiting cylindrical symmetry; axially symmetric
Less than normally active.
examples: Men have the naturally higher sex drive, yet all the laws, customs, punishments, shame, strictures, mystiques, and anti-mystiques are aimed at that tepid, sleepy, hypoactive creature the female libido.

senses: To rumple, tousle.
To pull to pieces.
ety: From Middle English tousen, tusen, from Old English *tūsian, from Proto-West Germanic *tūsōn. Cognate with German zausen (“to tousle”). Related also to English tease and toase. (a noisy disturbance): Compare typologically Russian раздра́й (razdráj) (<… драть (dratʹ)).
examples: How did he like it when the live creatures Tickled and toused and browsed him all over, And worm, slug, eft, with serious features Came in, each one, for his right of trover?
